film-83533.text: Avatar: Fire and Ash is overall an entertaining and occasionally tense film, but it clearly suffers from its excessive runtime. Many scenes drag on longer than necessary, which makes parts of the film feel boring despite its spectacle. There are some emotional moments, especially the scene where a father nearly kills his own son but ultimately can’t go through with it. The ending, with the general seemingly falling to his death, feels dramatic but far from final. Knowing this franchise, it’s hard to believe he won’t return in the next installment. Story-wise, the film closely mirrors the first two entries. The original Avatar was stronger despite its simple plot because the world was still new and the visual quality was groundbreaking for its time — and it still holds up today. The Way of Water felt like a repetition with a few emotional highlights. This third entry is slightly stronger than the second for me, but still far from special. There are no major plot twists and no particularly bold or masterfully written story elements. One watch is more than enough — this isn’t a film that benefits from rewatches. ⭐️⭐️⭐️ / 5
Liked it more than the last one but still the same story once again

film-76600.text: Avatar: The Way of Water is visually impressive, but beyond that, the film offers very little that feels new or engaging. The runtime is excessive, and many scenes feel stretched without adding real depth to the story or characters. Emotionally, there are moments that are clearly meant to hit hard — especially the death of a son — but even those scenes feel calculated rather than genuinely earned. The emotional impact is there on paper, but it never fully lands. Story-wise, the film repeats the same formula already used in the first Avatar, just relocated to a new environment. While the underwater visuals are stunning, they can’t compensate for the lack of narrative progression. Everything feels familiar, predictable, and safe. Overall, the film relies heavily on spectacle while neglecting strong storytelling. It’s too long, too repetitive, and offers little reason to return. One watch is more than enough. ⭐️⭐️½ / 5
Same thing again but even worse

film-694.text: The Shining is undeniably an important and well-crafted film, but the extended cut makes it feel noticeably long. Many scenes drag on, and traditional tension is sparse — the film relies far more on atmosphere than on sustained suspense. Instead of being gripping, it often feels distant. There’s a constant sense that something is wrong, but the film takes its time getting there. That slow-burn approach is deliberate and effective on a technical level, but not always engaging. Still, the film remains iconic, with unforgettable imagery, strong performances, and massive influence on the horror genre. It’s a film you admire more than you enjoy. I’d only rewatch it to show it to someone who hasn’t seen it before. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ / 5

film-501170.text: Doctor Sleep isn’t a bad film, but it often feels like a constant reminder of how great The Shining was. Many scenes feel less like independent storytelling and more like deliberate references designed to trigger nostalgia. The film is generally rewatchable, but it works much better if you already know The Shining. Ideally, you’d even watch the original first when showing Doctor Sleep to someone who hasn’t seen it yet. What’s most disappointing is the wasted emotional potential. Death and loss — involving both adults and children — are barely processed. Grief feels shallow or almost nonexistent, which creates emotional distance and weakens several key moments. Even Ewan McGregor, who is usually a very strong actor, feels underused here. Whether it’s the script or the direction is hard to say, but emotional scenes that should carry real weight simply don’t land. For example, when Dan’s friend — someone he had known for around eight years — dies, there’s barely any mourning: a brief look at the body, almost a tear, and then the film just moves on. In the end, Doctor Sleep is a solid and occasionally interesting film that relies too heavily on the legacy of its predecessor and never fully realizes its own potential. Rewatch: possible, but mainly for context or as a companion piece. ⭐️⭐️⭐️½ / 5

film-1062722.text: In my opinion, this is one of the best Frankenstein adaptations out there. The film is highly entertaining, fairly brutal, and unapologetically bloody — which actually adds a sense of realism rather than feeling excessive. What really stands out is how the monster is portrayed. It’s not just pure evil this time. The film makes a clear effort to show it as human: capable of emotions, inner conflict, loneliness, anger, and despair. That humanity makes the character far more compelling and tragic, and it’s what elevates the film beyond a standard horror adaptation. The balance between horror, drama, and character work is strong. It’s accessible, emotionally grounded, and feels more complete than many other versions of the story. Definitely a film that holds up on repeat viewings. Rewatch: yes, rewatchable ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ / 5

film-1228710.text:
Not as bad as I thought honestly.
I had very low expectations going into this movie and even lower ones after the first trailer, even though the later trailers definitely looked more promising. And then after all the reviews saying “Star Wars is dead” and stuff like that, my expectations were basically at zero. I genuinely expected to leave the cinema disappointed and regret watching it.
But honestly… I actually enjoyed it. I had fun, laughed a few times and especially the opening scene with the sun, the X-Wings and the music together with the Mandalorian & Grogu intro was really great.

Sadly the movie got weaker afterwards. I have to admit I didn’t really care that much about Jabba’s son as a character, so the middle part dragged a bit for me. The scene where Din Djarin falls into the water and fights that giant creature was really cool though. But overall the movie definitely slowed down too much in the middle before getting better again towards the end.
The cinematography and soundtrack were honestly amazing throughout the whole movie. I just kinda hoped we would get more of Din Djarin and Grogu fighting against the Empire like in the first hour because that stuff was easily the most fun part for me. But at the same time I understand why they couldn’t really introduce a huge main villain yet since characters like Thrawn are clearly being saved for Ahsoka Season 2 and the bigger movie later on. But at this point they honestly should’ve just not made it a movie.

I also thought it was really cool seeing Zeb from Rebels in live action again together with the X-Wing pilot from the first Mandalorian seasons. And the little Dave Filoni cameos were nice too 
A post-credit scene still would’ve been really nice though.

Overall I definitely enjoyed the movie and don’t regret watching it at all. It’s obviously not a masterpiece and I never expected it to be one. But it’s also nowhere near as terrible as some people make it out to be.
Can you skip the movie? Honestly yeah, kinda 😭 it basically feels like a 4-episode side quest at times. But despite that it was still entertaining and definitely rewatchable for me.
And let’s be real, nobody seriously expected this to come close to Episodes 1–6, Rogue One or Andor anyway.

⭐⭐⭐½ / 𝟓

film-969681.text:
Wow I expected a lot from this movie. The trailer honestly didn’t impress me that much because there were so many characters, and I had no idea how they were gonna make all of them work. I really thought it was gonna feel overcrowded.
But wow I absolutely loved this movie. Peak. Just peak. This is easily the best Spider-Man movie, including the other two Spider-Men.

It was so nice to finally get that street-level feeling again with Spider-Man fighting Scorpion and Tombstone. This was also the first time Peter really felt like he was on his own without someone constantly telling him what to do. The cinematography, the stunts, the camera work everything was fantastic. The cameos were amazing too. Bruce Banner was great, but Jon Bernthal was absolutely the goat. I honestly didn’t think Punisher would fit into a movie that wasn’t R-rated like the shows, but he fit perfectly. His emotional scene at the end was incredible, and I really hope we get to see Spider-Man and Punisher together again.

Also, Tina from The Bear was great. And seeing the real Hulk again was awesome, and Jean Grey was probably one of my favorite parts of the movie. Her acting was fantastic, and I really liked her story. I also loved that Peter started becoming even more spider-like with his abilities.

Black Widow leading the New Avengers was a really cool surprise too, and that bathtub scene was hot asf. Seeing the Hand again was awesome since I know them from Daredevil, even though I’m still not exactly sure where they originally came from. I was hoping Daredevil would show up, but, I don’t think it would’ve fit this movie.
The whole storyline with Ned and MJ was beautiful and sad at the same time. That scene where Peter finds out MJ has a boyfriend and then swings through the rain without his suit was one of the most emotional scenes in the entire movie. Another one of my favorite scenes was Peter and Jean Grey inside his mind. That one was really sad.

I also loved the scene where Jean Grey controlled MJ. For a second I genuinely thought she remembered Peter, but then it started to feel a little too easy. The reveal afterwards was really well done. And the scene with Peter and Ned playing Legislate was just wholesome.
The ending felt pretty open, which I actually liked. We still don’t know what happened to Jean Grey or what’s gonna happen with Ned and MJ. I do think Ned will eventually remember Peter though, especially because of the handshake at the end and him saying Peter’s name.

The post-credit scene was really short and didn’t reveal much. My guess is that it’s just teasing Spider-Man being in space for the next Avengers movie or something like that.
4.5/5

—————— 𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄 𝐏𝐀𝐑𝐓: ——————
Six feet under is a really strong show and definitely one of the best series I’ve ever watched. For me, this was one of the most beautiful and emotional TV experiences ever. I’m pretty sure I’ve never cried as much for any other show as I did for this one. The best thing about the show is clearly the characters and the acting. I’ve said that a lot in my episode reviews, many times, but I’m still gonna say it again.

I started the show and honestly expected a lot, but I was a bit unsure because of the whole funeral home topic. I didn’t expect the series to be THIS good. It completely exceeded my expectations. I watched the whole show within one month. I’m pretty sure I watched a ton of episodes…

What makes the show so strong are the characters. They don’t feel like typical TV characters, they feel like real people. With all their flaws, contradictions, and bad decisions. You don’t always love them. You’re often annoyed. But that’s exactly what makes them believable.

The acting was genuinely insane, like wow. Peter Krause, Lauren Ambrose, Michael C. Hall, Frances Conroy, Rachel Griffiths… all ridiculously good actors, without glazing anyone. Especially in the final season. Maybe I’m forgetting someone, but the most important ones are definitely mentioned.

————————— 𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑: —————————

My favorite character is probably Nate, with David right after him. But I was the most attached to Nate, and he hit me the hardest throughout the whole series. Even though he was often a total asshole. He’s probably the best-written character in the show. I just really loved his character.

He’s not perfect at all, and there were so many moments where I straight-up hated him, but at the same time he’s also incredibly tragic and goes through so much every season. He’s the character who had to endure the most, and also the one who was acted the best.

But I also love David. I love his relationship with Keith and how the show portrayed his inner conflicts, especially topics like homosexuality, religion, fear of rejection, internalized homophobia, etc. All of that was done really, really well. Since episode 1, I just wanted him to end up happy, and luckily he did.

Claire is obviously amazing too. In season 5 I liked her the most. She finally has a normal boyfriend and a really nice one, in my opinion. But honestly she was great in every season, and you always hoped she would finally be happy… yet she either got cheated on or had a crazy boyfriend.

And now I’m gonna say something about every season:

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟏:
A very good season. A great introduction to the characters, and for me it’s the 4th best season of the whole series.

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟐:
Definitely weaker than season 1, but still good. I wasn’t a big Brenda fan this season, but the last episodes with Nate were very strong.

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟑:
Season 3 was one of the strongest seasons of the show for me and definitely Nate’s best season. His conflict with Lisa was the emotional center and carried the whole season. Even though I never completely loved Lisa as a character, her death still hit extremely hard. Especially for Nate, even though it often felt like he was never truly satisfied in that relationship.

Peter Krause was on a completely different level this season. You can see Nate slowly falling apart inside. He feels restless, overwhelmed, lost, and that’s exactly what makes him so tragic.

3x1 was an insanely strong start. The first minutes were pure tension. You didn’t know if Nate was dying, if he would survive, or if he would have permanent damage. That uncertainty immediately made it clear this season was going to be emotional.

But 3x13 was a whole different league. The scene with Claire and Nathaniel, where she sees all the dead people, was surreal and at the same time beautifully directed. And then of course the bar scene with Nate. How he lets himself get beaten up, gets into the car bleeding, and his dad tells him during the drive that he should die. And Nate keeps repeating: “I don’t wanna die.”

That wasn’t some loud dramatic scene. That was a complete breakdown. And that’s exactly why it was so strong. For me, one of the most intense scenes in the entire show.

Season 3 is overall my 3rd favorite season of the series.

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟒:
Season 4 is my 2nd favorite season of the whole show. Especially 4x1 and 4x12 are absolute masterpieces.

4x1 was atmospherically insane. The scene where Nate buries Lisa is one of the best moments in the entire show for me. The silence, the emptiness, the desperation, and then Nate’s scream… it wasn’t just emotional, it was almost crushing. Peter Krause’s acting in that scene was phenomenal. That scene stays in your head.

4x12 is almost on the same level. Here Nate finally gets the truth about Lisa. Hoyt admits he had an affair with her. And then he realizes his wife heard everything, and he shoots himself right in front of Nate and right in front of his wife.

What makes that scene so strong isn’t just the shock. It’s the question that remains after. Did Hoyt kill himself because he couldn’t handle the guilt? Or because he knew he was actually responsible for Lisa’s death? The show doesn’t give a clear answer, and that’s exactly why it hits so hard. That’s why I love the scene too. It leaves room for interpretation and feels even more realistic because of it.

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟓:
Obviously the best season of the show. I love so much about it, but I especially want to talk about this end-run. The last 4 episodes were absolutely insane. They were so good that I need to talk about each one individually:

𝐄𝐂𝐎𝐓𝐎𝐍𝐄 – 𝟓𝐱𝟗
Nate’s death in “Ecotone” really got me. I was sure he would die at some point, but I thought it would happen in the finale. That hospital period where nobody knows if he’ll make it was insanely stressful and emotional. It was so sad that I almost cried already, especially when Claire cried. And I felt so bad for Ruth, because she couldn’t see him alive one last time. That was brutal. I feel so sorry for her.

“Everyone’s Waiting”… holy shit. I’ve never felt something like this in any other show. The scene where everyone sits at a table and eats together one last time was really beautiful. Every character got a perfect conclusion. David facing and accepting his trauma, Claire driving to New York… even though if you think about it, that wasn’t truly her final scene. In the end part where Claire drives away, you see everyone’s ending, and I found that extremely emotional and sad. Everyone dies one after another. And Claire dies last, the way it should be… everyone was waiting for her.

And seriously, the very last scene… the images of Claire are shown, the last photo she took before leaving, the ones from her art phase, Keith and David’s wedding… then the camera moves to Claire. And she dies quietly, without suffering. I have to say it again: a perfect ending for every character. Everyone got closure, even Rico and Vanessa got closure. Every storyline was completed perfectly. Dexter, Stranger Things, or Game of Thrones can only dream of an ending like that. Their endings don’t even come close to this masterpiece.

So yeah, if any episode deserves a 10/10, it’s “Everyone’s Waiting” without any debate.

I watched this on Disney+, where Episode 18 is split into two parts (18 & 19). I don’t know why it’s not like that everywhere, but that’s why I’m splitting my review into both parts:

𝐏𝐀𝐑𝐓 𝟏:
Perfect episode and already a perfect start to the ending of Scrubs. Right from the beginning, the music with the small flashbacks of J.D. and Turk was beautiful.

The scene where J.D. gives Dr. Cox a book filled with all his insults was really cool. Also the moment where Dr. Kelso says goodbye to J.D. was great, and of course the ending of this part, where Cox gives J.D. one final speech.
9.7/10

𝐏𝐀𝐑𝐓 𝟐:
Finally, J.D. admits that he put the penny in the door all those years ago. And he also finally learns the Janitor’s real name… or at least he thinks he does.

The most beautiful scene was definitely when Dr. Cox finally shows his true feelings for J.D. That was really emotional, and J.D. finally gets his hug.

And then the ending… for me, this is the best ending the show could’ve had. Seeing J.D. walk down the hallway and all the people from his past appear again was amazing. And then the moment where he stands in front of the white screen, imagining his future… just wow.

With the song “The Book of Love”, it was absolutely perfect.
There was also a small cameo by Bill Lawrence, which was really nice.

On Disney+, there were also behind-the-scenes clips showing how everything was filmed and when, which was a really cool extra.

For exactly these reasons, I have to give this episode a 10/10. It’s an emotional masterpiece and one of the best series finales of all time.

Went into this show with zero expectations and no clue what it was even about, and I definitely didn’t expect to enjoy it this much. I got hooked basically from the first episode, and it just kept getting better throughout the first three seasons. 

I loved how the show could completely change its tone without it feeling weird. It could be hilarious and then suddenly get dark, sometimes really dark. Especially in the later seasons, it went in directions I never would’ve expected when I first started watching it.
The characters were also a huge part of why I liked it so much. Barry, Gene, Fuches, Hank and Sally were all great, and the acting was incredible. Bill Hader especially was amazing as Barry.

Season 3 was definitely the peak of the show for me, but Season 2 was really close. Season 2 would’ve probably been even closer if it wasn’t for that one episode that dragged it down a bit. Season 3 was just insanely consistent and had some of the best episodes of the entire show, including the finale, which is still my favorite episode.

Season 4 was probably my least favorite season, but I still really enjoyed it. It felt pretty different from the other seasons, but I really liked how everything ended. I couldn’t imagine a better ending for the show.

The Bear is easily one of the best TV shows I’ve ever watched. It’s in my Top 15. What makes this show so special isn’t just the incredible writing or cinematography, it’s the characters. Every single character feels like a real person with flaws, insecurities and personal struggles. What surprised me the most was how stressful the show could be without relying on action. A dinner service in The Bear is honestly more intense than entire action scenes in other shows.
The acting was phenomenal from beginning to end. Jeremy Allen White, Ayo Edebiri, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Jamie Lee Curtis, Jon Bernthal, Bob Odenkirk, and the rest of the cast were all incredible. The soundtrack was amazing too, and the cinematography was beautiful throughout the entire series.

Most importantly, The Bear actually managed to stick the landing. After so many disappointing series finales, it was refreshing to watch a show that gave its characters the ending they deserved.

—————— 𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑 ——————

The biggest strength of this show has always been its characters. Carmy, Richie and Sydney carried the series for me, but honestly, almost every character had fantastic development. Richie probably had my favorite character arc in the entire show. Watching him slowly find confidence and purpose again was really satisfying. Donna was another huge highlight. Jamie Lee Curtis gave one of the best performances in the series, especially in “Fishes,” which is still one of my favorite TV episodes of all time.

Seasons 1 and 2 were nearly perfect. Both seasons were fantastic. Season 3 was definitely the weakest season for me, but Seasons 4 and especially 5 brought the show right back. Season 5 reminded me why I fell in love with this series in the first place. The intensity was finally back, almost every episode had me completely invested, and the finale was exactly how you end a TV show.
I’ll definitely miss spending time with these characters.

⚠️ 𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐁𝐄𝐋𝐎𝐖⚠️ 

I’m not really sure how to feel about this episode.
The first 30–40 minutes were honestly really good. Everything involving Jax was emotional and I really liked seeing more of his backstory. The scenes between Pomni and Jax, especially with Isn’t She Lovely by Stevie Wonder playing, were easily my favorite part of the episode.

But after that, I was honestly disappointed.
After the ending of the last episode, I expected everything to completely fall apart. I thought we’d finally get the huge payoff, with everyone trying to escape while everything was collapsing around them. Instead, it felt like the story suddenly slowed down again. It honestly reminded me of the jump from the Stranger Things Season 4 finale to Season 5.
Even though I liked all the scenes with Jax, why did they spend more than half the episode focusing on him, only to move on with the main story and barely mention him again? And the fact that Jax just abstracted off-screen was really disappointing.

What confused me the most was the explanation itself. Maybe I misunderstood parts of it, but a lot of it just didn’t make much sense to me.
If these are supposed to be AI copies based on real people’s minds, how did that even happen? How did they get those minds in the first place? Do the real people still live normal lives while these versions are trapped in the circus? If that’s the case, why doesn’t anyone really question it?

I also still don’t understand what happens to the abstracted characters. Are they just trapped forever now? And why does Jax remember parts of his old life but nothing after that? He only remembers the scene in the car, but nothing after it. It’s almost like his mind was transferred into the game at that exact moment but how would that even be possible?
I feel like there are just too many unanswered questions. The whole company and experiment storyline seemed like it was building toward something much bigger, but instead it just left me even more confused.

I really wanted to love this finale because the emotional moments were great, but after the first half it felt like the episode was rushing through ideas instead of properly explaining them.

“Whatever happens… I’ll always be by your side…”

That opening flashback with Kinger and his wife was insane. Especially emotionally, because it really feels like they knew each other in real life. It gives the vibe that he might’ve been the one who helped create all of this. Maybe he built the AI and entered the system with her, like some kind of experiment.

And maybe Cratch wanted just that because of his brain tumor. An alternative world with an AI where he can't die. That would be really intense and would explain a lot.
Also the concept that when Kinger is surrounded by darkness, his true mind comes back? That’s such a cool and interesting idea.

Every scene with Caine was just insane. Especially that song from Caine was really good, it gave off such strong villain vibes. Lowkey reminded me of Bowser, just this over-the-top, slightly chaotic evil energy that somehow still feels fun to watch.
Also him losing control in the office and then basically torturing everyone at the end… yeah that was dark. And that line “where is Kinger?” coming from an AI like that? Actually creepy.

And then the ending… Kinger deleting Caine?? What the hell. I thought the last episode already had a crazy cliffhanger, but this was on another level. Now everything is about to fall apart. With Caine gone, there are no rules anymore. The abstracted ones are no longer contained, and even worse, no one can be healed or reset now.
This is actually insane… and now we have to wait months for the finale.

„Was auch immer passiert… ich werde immer an deiner Seite sein…“

Dieser Rückblick direkt am Anfang mit Kinger und seiner Frau war wirklich krass. Vor allem emotional, weil es so wirkt, als hätten sie sich im echten Leben gekannt. Es fühlt sich so an, als hätte er vielleicht selbst an dieser ganzen Sache mitgearbeitet. Vielleicht hat er die KI entwickelt und ist dann zusammen mit ihr in dieses System gegangen, wie so ein Experiment.

Und vielleicht wollte Cratch wegen seinem Gehirntumor genau das haben. Eine alternative Welt mit einer KI wo er nicht sterben kann. Das wäre wirklich heftig und würde vieles erklären.
Auch den Fant, dass Kinger, wenn er nichts sieht und nur Dunkelheit hat, wieder seinen klaren Verstand bekommt, ist richtig geil und interessant.

Alle Szenen mit Caine waren komplett crazy. 
Vor allem dieser Song von Caine war echt geil, der hatte richtig krasse Bösewicht-Vibes. Hat mich ein bisschen an Bowser erinnert, dieses übertriebene, leicht chaotische Evil, das trotzdem irgendwie Spaß macht zuzusehen.
Und wie er im Büro komplett durchdreht und am Ende alle foltert… das war schon sehr düster. Und dieser Satz „where is Kinger?“ aus dem Mund einer KI ist schon echt gruselig.

Und dann das Ende… Kinger löscht einfach Caine?? Was zur Hölle. Ich dachte schon die letzte Folge war ein krasser Cliffhanger, aber das hier toppt nochmal alles. Jetzt bricht ja komplett alles zusammen. Ohne Caine gibt es keine Regeln mehr, die abstrakten Monster sind nicht mehr eingesperrt und noch schlimmer ist, dass niemand mehr geheilt oder zurückgesetzt werden kann.
Das ist wirklich geisteskrank… und jetzt muss man Monate auf das Finale warten.

Definitely the weakest season of the show so far.
I still enjoyed it, but compared to the previous seasons, this one was a noticeable step down. There were still some great episodes and emotional moments, but the pacing became a real problem. Too many episodes felt like they were just setting things up instead of actually moving the story forward.
I was so hyped after the Season 3 finale because I thought we’d finally start getting some real answers. Instead, I finished this season with even more questions than before. After four seasons I really expected more progress.

I’m still looking forward to the final season, but nowhere near as much as I was before this one.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑𝐒——————

There were definitely some really good moments this season, but I feel like almost every answer created five new questions. After everything Season 3 set up, I expected much bigger payoffs. The Fatima storyline was probably the biggest surprise, but it didn’t go in the direction I expected at all.
The finale was honestly really disappointing. The storm, the Man in Yellow, the bones, Julie and Randall’s storyline, the Lake of Tears, the moving cabins so many plotlines either went nowhere or still haven’t been explained.

The biggest problem is that the show keeps ending episodes with huge cliffhangers, only for the next episode to immediately slow everything down again. At this point, I just want answers instead of more mysteries.
Season 5 definitely has potential, especially after everything that happened in the finale, but I’ve honestly lost a lot of confidence that every mystery will get a satisfying explanation.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

Season 1 is honestly just peak television. For me, it’s one of the best first seasons ever made.
Everything feels raw and grounded. The atmosphere is insane, the pacing is slower but in a good way, and the tension is always there. It doesn’t rely on constant action, it builds its world and characters first, and that’s exactly why it works so well.

You really feel how dangerous this world is right from the start. The walkers aren’t just background threats, they feel unpredictable and actually scary.

What also stands out is how quickly you get invested in the characters. Even early on, you already care about what happens to them, which is rare for a first season.
Not every episode is perfect, there are some slower moments, but even those stay interesting because of the strong atmosphere and character focus.

Overall, an insanely strong start that still holds up as one of the best beginnings of any show.

Rick waking up in the hospital is still one of the best openings ever. That whole sequence just pulls you in instantly. And then moments like Morgan not being able to shoot his wife… yeah, that hits every single time.

The Atlanta storyline is iconic. Glenn’s introduction alone is legendary. And scenes like Rick riding into the city on the horse just feel so cinematic.

The character dynamics are where the season really shines. Shane vs Rick already starts building here, and you can clearly see how different they are. Shane is way more emotional and aggressive, while Rick still tries to hold onto his morals. That contrast is perfect
Also small dynamics like Dale & Andrea or Shane & Carl feel very real and grounded.

The Vatos episode is actually underrated, especially with the twist at the end. And then the CDC arc… such a different setting, but it works. Dr. Jenner adds a completely new perspective to the outbreak, and the whole finale just feels heavy and emotional.
That last scene with the explosion and the music… perfect ending.

Season 1 just has that special feeling. Everything is new, everything is dangerous, and knowing what happens later makes a lot of these moments hit even harder.

From Jon Bernthal’s acting to the writing of his character, everything about Shane is just insane to watch. He feels raw, real, and way ahead of everyone else at that point.
What’s crazy is that if Shane had shown up a few seasons later, everyone would already be like him. He would’ve fit perfectly next to Rick in his later seasons. In a way, Shane was just early.

This was also back when The Walking Dead wasn’t afraid to take risks. This moment was necessary to push Shane’s arc forward and show how far he’s willing to go.
It’s a dark turn, but it feels very realistic. What Shane does is clearly wrong, but at the same time, you understand why he thinks it’s necessary. That’s what makes it so strong.

Cold, brutal, but incredibly well written I just love it.

And of course, the legendary scene of Rick riding his horse into Atlanta. What an incredibly cinematic and powerful moment. Beautiful and terrifying at the same time. Those early season vibes are unmatched. Seeing Rick in his sheriff uniform, still innocent and hopeful, just hits differently.

And then the ending:

„Hey, you dumbass.
Yeah, you in the tank.
You cozy in there?“

Glenn’s first words. Iconic.

And closing it all with “Space Junk” was perfect. That song fits the mood so well. I love it.

A nearly fantastic second season overall. I still think Season 1 was stronger, mainly because the story felt more focused, but Season 2 still delivered some incredible moments. The action was once again amazing and some of the fight scenes were among the best in the entire show.
What held the season back a little for me was that it sometimes felt split between two very different storylines. One of them was consistently great, while the other never fully clicked with me.

Overall though, this was still a really strong season with great action, strong character work and some fantastic episodes.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

The biggest reason why I enjoyed this season so much was definitely Frank Castle.
Every storyline involving the Punisher was amazing. Whether it was the cemetery scenes, the prison storyline or the finale, Jon Bernthal absolutely stole the show whenever he appeared. What made Frank so interesting wasn’t just that he was a badass, but that his arguments against Matt often actually made sense. 

Matt was great again this season, but unlike Season 1 it often felt like the show was almost being shared between Matt and Frank. And honestly, I didn’t mind that at all because their dynamic was incredible.
Unfortunately the Hand storyline never reached the same level for me. I liked Elektra and her chemistry with Matt, but the whole Black Sky storyline was definitely the weakest part of the season. Even by the finale I still wasn’t completely sure I understood what the Hand was actually trying to achieve.

The finale itself was really good. The rooftop scenes, Punisher helping Daredevil against the ninjas, Karen’s speech and Matt finally telling Karen the truth were all great moments. Elektra’s death honestly didn’t hit me that hard emotionally, but the ending definitely made me curious about where her story is going next.

Overall I think Season 2 peaks whenever Frank and Matt or Frank and Karen share the screen together. Matt and Frank gave us some of the best philosophical discussions in the entire show, while Frank and Karen brought out a much more emotional and human side of his character.

༆ 𝐃𝐀𝐑𝐄𝐃𝐄𝐕𝐈𝐋 – 𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟏 ༆

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

What a great first season. Daredevil Season 1 honestly surprised me a lot and is definitely one of the strongest first seasons of any superhero show I’ve seen.
Right from the beginning I really liked Matt Murdock as a character. The whole concept of being a lawyer during the day and a vigilante at night is already cool by itself, but the fact that he’s blind and still does all of this makes him even more interesting. His backstory was also really emotional and well written.

The atmosphere of the show was amazing too. It felt dark, grounded and brutal the entire time. The fight scenes especially were insane and felt way more raw and realistic than most superhero shows.
But the biggest surprise for me was definitely Wilson Fisk. He’s easily one of the best Marvel villains I’ve seen so far. Not just because he’s so cold and intimidating, but because the show actually makes him feel human too. I also really liked the side characters and dynamics this season. Foggy and Karen were both great and added a lot to the emotional side of the show. Claire Temple was also a really good addition and her dynamic with Matt was very enjoyable.

Overall this season had amazing action, great characters, emotional moments and a really strong atmosphere from beginning to end.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

The whole storyline between Matt and Fisk was absolutely incredible. Every interaction between them had so much tension even before they truly met face to face.
One of the biggest highlights of the season was definitely Fisk’s backstory. Seeing how abusive his father was and then watching Fisk kill him was genuinely brutal and honestly one of the craziest moments of the season.

The fights this season were also absolutely insane. Matt vs Nobu, Matt vs Fisk, the hallway fights, all of them felt brutal and realistic. And the fight in the finale with Matt finally wearing the Daredevil suit was just peak.
The emotional side of the season was also really strong. Foggy finding out that Matt is the man in the mask was a huge moment and you could really feel how betrayed and shocked he was. The conversations between Matt and the priest were also amazing and added a lot to Matt’s character and morality.

And then Ben Urich’s death… yeah that was crazy. I genuinely thought Fisk would just threaten him, not actually kill him. That moment really showed how dangerous Fisk truly is despite all his more human moments throughout the season.
The finale was honestly perfect too. Fisk escaping, the corrupt FBI agents and cops helping him, Matt finally becoming Daredevil, and then Fisk ending up in prison while Nelson & Murdock rebuild their office again… it was just a really perfect ending.

༆ 𝐏𝐄𝐑𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝐎𝐅 𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐄𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐓 ༆

One of the greatest and most underrated shows I have ever seen. Easily T8 OAT for me.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

I honestly didn’t expect this show to become what it became. At first it almost feels like a normal procedural crime show with a cool concept: a billionaire and an ex-CIA agent trying to save people. But over time the show evolves into something so much bigger than that.
By the end it’s not really just about stopping crimes anymore. It becomes a story about humanity, choices, sacrifice and how technology can change people and the world around them.

And what makes all of this even crazier is how the show evolves over time. In
The first season is definitely the weakest one for me, but that says more about how insane the later seasons become than about Season 1 itself. Every season constantly raises the stakes, gets more emotional and expands the world more and more until the show eventually turns into one of the best sci-fi thrillers I’ve ever watched.

What I especially love about Person of Interest is that it never forgets its characters. Even when the story becomes much bigger later on, the emotional core of the show always stays the relationships between the characters.
I would genuinely recommend this show to everyone who enjoys sci-fi thrillers, AI themes, action and emotional character-driven stories. But I can also understand why the show might not be for everyone. Especially the beginning is much slower and more procedural compared to the later seasons.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

One of the biggest reasons why I loved this show so much were the characters and the dynamics between them.

Harold Finch is honestly one of the best written TV characters ever for me. Watching him slowly lose faith in his own rules after everything he sacrificed and everything he lost was incredible. His philosophical conflict throughout the show is genuinely fascinating because he constantly struggles between morality and necessity.

“I have played by the rules for so long.”

That monologue alone already proves how incredible his character writing was.

John Reese was amazing as well. He starts the show as a broken man with nothing left to live for, but through Finch, the team and the Machine he slowly rediscovers the value of life and purpose again. His development throughout the series was honestly beautiful to watch and his ending was perfect for his character.

Root was another incredible character overall. At first she almost feels completely insane, but over time she becomes one of the emotional cores of the series. Her connection to the Machine was honestly beautiful and the decision to let the Machine continue with her voice after her death was genuinely genius writing. She was also one of the most entertaining characters in the entire show and brought such a unique energy whenever she appeared.

Shaw’s development was amazing too. She starts as someone emotionally disconnected from everyone around her, but slowly learns to care because of the team, especially Root. Some of the most emotional moments in the show honestly came from her character and her relationship with Root was one of the best dynamics in the series.

And then there’s Fusco… honestly one of the best character developments in the entire show. He starts as a dirty cop and slowly becomes one of the purest and most loyal people in the series. Him finally becoming a full member of the team felt completely earned. At first he was mostly there to help Reese and Finch from the sidelines, but over time he became one of the most important and loyal members of the team.

Finch and Reese are honestly one of the greatest duos in television history for me. Their relationship slowly evolving from employer and employee into genuine friendship and brotherhood was honestly one of the best dynamics in television for me. They constantly changed each other throughout the series and the ending of their story together was heartbreaking and perfect at the same time.
Finch and the Machine also became one of the most interesting relationships in the entire show. At first the Machine simply feels like a tool, but over time their relationship becomes surprisingly emotional, especially in the later seasons.

Root and Shaw easily had one of the best relationships in the series too. At first their dynamic is mostly funny, but over time it becomes genuinely emotional. Watching Shaw slowly learn to care about Root was honestly beautiful.

Reese and Fusco were also one of the funniest and most underrated duos in the show. They start off barely trusting each other, but over time become genuinely loyal friends.

And Reese together with Carter probably had some of the most emotional scenes in the entire series because Carter was one of the first people who truly believed Reese could still be a good person.

The AI philosophy in this show is honestly way ahead of its time too. The conflict between the Machine and Samaritan isn’t just “good AI vs evil AI.” It’s really about freedom vs control. The Machine values human choice while Samaritan believes humanity needs to be controlled for its own survival. And the scary part is that Samaritan’s logic sometimes actually makes sense. Greer was such a phenomenal antagonist because he genuinely believed he was saving humanity. 
He wasn’t evil for the sake of being evil, he truly believed order mattered more than freedom.

Of course I also have to mention some negatives. The most obvious flaws were definitely the occasional plot armor and the acting at times. As much as I love this show, some performances honestly felt a bit emotionless sometimes 😭 especially Reese’s actor, who occasionally just stood there staring into the distance like a scarecrow.
Personally it never really bothered me that much because the writing, characters and emotional moments were strong enough to make up for it, but I still wanted to mention it.

And honestly the emotional damage this show causes is crazy 😭

Carter’s death.
Root’s death.
Reese’s sacrifice.
The Devil’s Share.
Terra Incognita.
“If you can hear this…”

This show genuinely destroyed me emotionally multiple times.

Now I’m gonna talk a little bit about every season individually even though I already did that in my season reviews.

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟏:
A really strong introduction to the world and characters even though it’s definitely the weakest season overall. The procedural structure worked surprisingly well because Reese and Finch already carried the show hard from the beginning. Elias was also such a great antagonist and the finale with Firewall and God Mode was amazing.
Overall my least favorite season, but still very enjoyable.
⭐⭐⭐⭐ / 𝟓 · 𝟖.𝟕/𝟏𝟎

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟐:
This is where the show really starts becoming something bigger. The world expands massively and the show slowly starts diving deeper into its AI and surveillance themes. Root becomes one of the most interesting characters in the show and Shaw was also a really great addition.
⭐⭐⭐⭐ / 𝟓 · 𝟖.𝟗/𝟏𝟎

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟑:
Season 3 is where the show becomes actual peak television. The emotional moments hit way harder, the stakes constantly rise and the writing becomes insane. Easily my T2 season of the show.
The whole HR storyline was incredible and Carter’s death genuinely shocked me. The Devil’s Share is honestly one of the best revenge/emotional episodes I’ve ever watched.

But then the final run with The Crossing, The Devil’s Share and Deus Ex Machina… that was absolute peak television. The ending of Deus Ex Machina with Exit Music (For a Film) playing was genuinely one of the greatest scenes in the entire series.
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ / 𝟓 · 𝟗.𝟖/𝟏𝟎

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟒:
Season 4 is probably the darkest season overall. The vibe feels very different compared to the earlier seasons and the whole season has a much heavier atmosphere. Everything just feels way more intense and serious now.
If-Then-Else was honestly one of the most unique and creative TV episodes I’ve ever seen. I genuinely can’t think of another episode like it. Also, the subway simulation reveal was insane.

Terra Incognita was another incredible episode because it gave Reese one of the most emotional episodes in the entire series. Him hallucinating Carter throughout the episode was heartbreaking, even though it’s considered a filler episode.
And then there’s YHWH… probably one of the most intense episodes in the whole show.
⭐⭐⭐⭐½ / 𝟓 · 𝟗.𝟔/𝟏𝟎

𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟓:
Honestly one of the greatest final seasons ever made. The emotional impact of this season was insane. Episodes like The Day the World Went Away, .exe, Sotto Voce and especially return 0 were absolute peak television.

Elias’ death honestly hit me way harder than I expected. He was easily one of the best and most entertaining characters in the entire show and the fact that this time he was actually gone made it even sadder.
Root’s death was heartbreaking too, but at the same time weirdly perfect for her character because the Machine continuing with her voice afterwards fit her perfectly.

And Finch this season… wow.

“I have played by the rules for so long.”

That monologue against Samaritan was easily one of the greatest scenes in the entire show.
But obviously the biggest highlight was the finale itself.

“When you came to me, you gave me a job. A purpose.”

That rooftop conversation between Finch and Reese completely broke me. Reese sacrificing himself for Finch and for the world was honestly the perfect ending for his character.
The final Machine monologue, the soundtrack, the rooftop sequence, Shaw visiting Root’s grave, Finch finally getting peace… I genuinely don’t think they could’ve ended the show any better than this.
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ / 𝟓 · 𝟏𝟎/𝟏𝟎

What makes Person of Interest so special to me is that it constantly evolves without ever losing its emotional core. The show starts as a procedural crime thriller and slowly turns into something much bigger. A story about humanity, surveillance, freedom, sacrifice and what it truly means to care about people. And despite all the AI themes and philosophical questions, the thing that always mattered most were the characters and their relationships with each other.

Very few shows manage to balance action, emotion, philosophy and character writing this well while also constantly getting better with every season.
The finale especially proved how much the writers understood these characters. Every important character got a satisfying conclusion and the ending somehow managed to feel tragic, emotional, hopeful and beautiful at the same time.

Person of Interest honestly deserves way more recognition because for me this wasn’t just another sci-fi show. It became one of the most emotional and unforgettable television experiences I’ve ever had.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

Season 5 is honestly one of the best final seasons I’ve ever seen. From the very first episode you can already feel that everything is coming to an end and the atmosphere throughout the whole season is incredible because of that.
The stakes are at their absolute highest now and this is definitely the best season of the entire show for me.

What makes this season so special is how emotional and intense it feels compared to the previous seasons. Nearly every episode feels important and there’s constantly this feeling that everything could collapse at any moment.

The pacing was also surprisingly great for a final season with only 13 episodes. It almost never felt rushed to me.
The soundtrack and writing were incredible too. You can really tell the writers knew exactly how they wanted to end the show.

Honestly… this season just felt different.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

This season was genuinely heartbreaking.
Elias’ death honestly hit me way harder than I expected. He was easily one of the best and most entertaining characters in the entire show and the fact that this time he was actually gone made it even sadder. His final moments together with Finch were incredible too. Shaw finally returning after all the simulations was such a great moment.

Episodes like Sotto Voce, The Day the World Went Away, .exe and especially return 0 were absolute peak television and honestly some of the best episodes in the entire series.

Root’s death honestly hurt so much, but at the same time it weirdly felt perfect for her character. The fact that the Machine literally continues with her voice after she dies was one of the best decisions the writers could’ve made. It fit her character perfectly because throughout the whole show she always wanted to become closer to the Machine.
And Finch this season… wow. His entire breakdown after losing everyone and finally abandoning his old moral code was insane to watch. That monologue in The Day the World Went Away was easily one of the best scenes in the entire show.

“I have played by the rules for so long.”

That entire scene was just incredible. Finch finally stops following his own rules and finally uses the Machine the way he should’ve done a long time ago.
Greer was also amazing this season. Completely insane and genuinely terrifying because he truly believed everything he was doing was right. And in the end he even sacrificed himself for Samaritan.

But obviously the biggest highlight of the season was the finale. return 0 is honestly one of the greatest finales I’ve ever seen. It might genuinely be a Top 2 finale of all time for me. The way the episode plays with time, the Machine slowly losing track of past and future, Reese sacrificing himself and the emotional ending for every major character… it was all perfect.

“When you came to me, you gave me a job. A purpose.”

That rooftop conversation between Finch and Reese was heartbreaking and perfectly showed how much Reese changed throughout the entire series.
I genuinely don’t think they could’ve ended the show any better than this.

PEAK. Honestly a perfect ending, I genuinely don’t think they could’ve done it any better.

Right at the beginning of the episode the Machine starts talking and explaining everything, and then with that music and the scene of Harold on the rooftop… you basically see the ending of the episode and therefore the ending of the entire show immediately. But at first you understand almost nothing. Harold is seemingly shot, the world is collapsing because of the virus and the Machine itself appears to be dying too.
What I absolutely loved is how the episode plays with time because the Machine itself no longer fully understands what is past and what is future. At first you only see fragments of the ending and then slowly the episode shows how everything actually led up to that point. It was honestly genius.

At first I even thought Fusco had died and that the boy at the grave was his son 😭 but later you realize it was actually John Reese standing at his father’s grave.

What also made this finale so incredible is how personal it felt for every character. Shaw finally going to Root’s grave and saying goodbye was such a perfect moment for her.
Then after Finch uploads the virus onto the server where Samaritan’s backup was being uploaded, he locks Reese away because he wants to sacrifice himself. But then comes the plot twist… when Finch finally reaches the rooftop in the present timeline, he realizes he’s on the wrong rooftop. Reese had made his own deal with the Machine.

Reese is the one who has to stop Samaritan because Samaritan is trying to upload itself onto a satellite to survive the virus, meaning someone has to manually align the satellite dish on the roof. And that’s where Root’s rocket plan finally comes into play. That reveal was actually insane.

“When you came to me, you gave me a job. A purpose.”

The entire rooftop sequence between Finch and Reese was perfect. The music, Metamorphosis One by Philip Glass, was genuinely one of the best song choices in the whole show.
That entire scene perfectly shows how much Reese changed throughout the series. In the beginning he was basically a dead man walking, but through Finch, the team and the Machine he slowly became someone who truly understood the value of life again.

Watching Reese fight off everyone sent by Samaritan while Finch walks away to safety was heartbreaking. And the Machine staying with John in Root’s form during his final moments made it even more emotional. The flashbacks to John as a child at his father’s funeral made the entire thing hit even harder because in the end John became exactly what he always admired: a real hero.
And then when the missile finally hits the building with Reese still there… man, that hurt. For a brief moment I also thought Fusco was about to die after getting stabbed, thank God he survived 😭

What makes this finale so special is that every important character gets a satisfying ending. Harold can finally return to Grace and live a normal life again after losing so much throughout the series. Shaw and Fusco both survive as well and finally get some sort of peace after everything they went through. Shaw even gets revenge for Root in the end, which made her final scenes even more satisfying and emotional. And then there’s the Machine itself… everyone believed she was gone, but that final reveal that she survived was honestly beautiful.

The cinematography and soundtrack were phenomenal too. This finale genuinely felt like perfection to me. Constant peaks from beginning to end. Easily one of the greatest finales ever made and one of my favorite TV episodes of all time, probably T5 for me.
Honestly I don’t even know what else to say. The ending was sad, beautiful and emotional all at the same time. But most of all… it’s just sad that the show is over now.

Wtf what a peak episode. Honestly one of the best episodes of the entire show.
First Elias dies… and this time he’s actually dead. That genuinely made me sad because he was one of my favorite characters in the whole series.
And then Root too… it was heartbreaking but at the same time kinda fitted because she already knew. You could tell during that conversation in the car with Finch that she understood what was coming. She wanted to convince him to finally do what’s necessary and truly work with the Machine.

And honestly her death was weirdly perfect because now the Machine literally has her voice. That fits so perfectly considering how much Root loved the Machine and always wanted to be connected to it somehow.
But the best scene in the episode and maybe one of the best scenes in the entire show was easily Finch’s monologue. Holy shit that was COLD.

———————————————————————————

Finch: “I have played by the rules for so long.”

Control: “Not from where I’m sitting.”

Finch: “No. Not your rules.

You work at the behest of a system so broken that you didn’t even notice when it became corrupted at its core.

When I first broke your rules, a sitting president had authorized assassination squads in Laos, and the head of the FBI had ordered his men — you — to conduct illegal surveillance on his political rivals.

Your rules have changed every time it was convenient for you.

I was talking about my rules.

I have lived by those rules for so long.

Believed in them for so long.

Believed that if you played by the right rules, eventually you would win.

But I was wrong, wasn’t I?

And now all the people I cared about are dead. Or will be dead soon enough.

And we will be gone without a trace.

So now I have to decide.

Decide whether to let my friends die, to let hope die, to let the world be ground under your heel all because I played by my rules.

I’m trying to decide.

I’m going to kill you.

But I need to decide how far I’m willing to go… how many of my own rules I’m willing to break to get it done.”

Control: “Look, you want to add threatening the life of a federal agent to your file, I will draw up those charges right now. No waiting is required.”

Finch: “I wasn’t talking to you.”

———————————————————————————

That whole scene was just insane. Finch finally stops following his own rules and finally uses the Machine the way he should’ve done a long time ago. The way he was directly talking to Samaritan there was just cool as hell.
And then that ending with the song The Day the World Went Away… exactly like the episode title..

Season 4 is easily one of the best seasons of the show so far. I think it’s the second best season overall. At this moment, my favorite season is still Season 3.
The stakes are way higher than before and the whole Samaritan storyline makes everything feel much more intense imo.

What I really liked is how the show balances action, emotional moments and character development. Even episodes that people might call “filler” still add something, especially to characters like John and Finch.
The Machine also became more important to the story this season and adds a lot to the overall tension and atmosphere.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

Samaritan was such a crazy antagonist this season. The fact that it’s always one step ahead and basically controls everything makes it feel almost unbeatable.
Episodes like If-Then-Else, YHWH and Terra Incognita were absolute peak. Especially how the Machine calculates thousands of outcomes or how John is basically on the edge of death… those episodes hit different imo.

The Dominic vs Elias storyline was also insanely good. Elias manipulating everything so Dominic destroys himself was just perfect. Still sad that Elias died, he was one of the best characters.
And the finale was just insane. The scene with Finch and the Machine (“father and child”) was one of the best moments of the entire show. Samaritan wiping out so many people and the Machine barely surviving in that suitcase… absolute peak.

༆ 𝐏𝐄𝐑𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝐎𝐅 𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐄𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐓 – 𝐒𝐄𝐀𝐒𝐎𝐍 𝟑 𝐑𝐄𝐕𝐈𝐄𝐖 ༆

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

Wow… what a season. This was by far the best season of the show so far imo. Compared to the first two seasons, you can now feel the bigger story in almost every single episode. It no longer feels like just “one case per episode”, the show now has a much stronger ongoing storyline and everything feels way more connected.

This season also had by far the best peaks of the series so far. Not just because of the action, but because of how emotional and intense everything became. It was honestly also the saddest season so far.

The storytelling, the backstories, the music and especially the atmosphere were all on another level this season. You could really feel that the stakes became much bigger with Samaritan, Vigilance, Decima and the government storyline.
And the music… wow. Easily the best soundtrack usage in the show so far.

Overall this season felt like Person of Interest fully evolving from a procedural show into something much bigger.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

The biggest peak of the season was the entire HR finale arc. Quinn was the perfect leader for HR, even though Simmons honestly felt even more cruel and dangerous. The comparison to Negan and Simon from The Walking Dead honestly fits really well.
And then right when it finally feels like HR is defeated and Carter is finally getting rewarded for everything… Simmons kills her. That was genuinely the saddest moment in the entire show so far.

Everything after that was incredible too. Reese completely losing himself after Carter’s death was extremely emotional and probably Jim Caviezel’s best acting in the series so far. Especially the scenes where he hunts down everyone connected to Simmons.

What makes it even sadder is that every time Reese truly starts caring about or loving someone, they die. First Jessica, where he arrived too late and couldn’t save her, and now Carter. You could really feel throughout Season 3 that Reese slowly started falling in love with her, and just when things finally started getting better between them, she dies too. That honestly makes Reese one of the most tragic characters in the entire show.

The Devil’s Share was also one of the most emotional episodes in the entire show. The opening alone with Reese searching for Simmons while Johnny Cash’s “Hurt” plays in the background was genuinely masterful.
The scene where Reese stands in front of Quinn covered in blood and tells him that he’ll kill him no matter what was insane. And then directly after that, seeing Reese almost collapse while trying to pull the trigger was such a strong moment.

But Fusco also played a huge role in why this arc was so emotional and strong. Seeing him get tortured by HR and almost losing his son made the whole storyline feel even more personal and brutal. And then later seeing Fusco break Simmons’ arm and drag him into the precinct while “Medicine” plays in the background was honestly one of the most satisfying moments in the series. I genuinely thought for a second they were going to let Simmons live, but then Elias kills him in the end. That honestly felt like the perfect ending for his character after everything he had done.

The third biggest peak of the season was the Samaritan hunt in episodes 3x11–12.

That entire storyline was incredibly intense because every group was after the machine at the same time. Finch, Reese, Shaw and Root were trying to destroy Samaritan with the help of Arthur Claypool, while Vigilance wanted to expose the existence of mass surveillance to the entire world. At the same time, Control was trying to secretly take Samaritan for the government before anyone else could get to it.

And then the plot twist… just when it looked like Finch had actually destroyed Samaritan, Greer reveals that Decima had already switched the drives beforehand through one of their agents. He once again planned everything ahead.
That whole arc was honestly one of the smartest and most exciting parts of the season.

And then finally the second biggest peak of the season: Deus Ex Machina and the ending arc.

The reveal that Greer had planned almost everything from the beginning was crazy. The fact that he basically created Vigilance and used Peter Collier for his own plan was such a good twist. Collier thought he was exposing the truth to the world while in reality nobody was even watching the trial.
That entire courtroom sequence with Finch, Greer and Control was perfect. Especially when Finch finally reveals himself as the creator of the Machine.

The Grace storyline was also extremely emotional. When Finch finds out that Greer kidnapped her and says:
“If they harm Grace in any way, kill them all.”
Yeah… that scene was perfect.

And then the final twist with Root and the servers. The whole time it looked like she was trying to destroy Samaritan, but instead she planned everything so that the seven members of the team would become invisible to Samaritan. Such a good ending.

The final scenes with everyone living under different identities while Samaritan controls the world, while “Exit Music (For a Film)” by Radiohead plays in the background, were honestly an incredible setup for Season 4.
This season was just peak television.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

I honestly can’t fully decide if Season 1 or 2 is better. Season 1 had the stronger finale in my opinion, but Season 2 had way more peaks overall.

One thing I really loved this season was the deeper storytelling. You can clearly see that the show is starting to build a bigger overall plot instead of just “one number per episode”, even though that concept is still there.
The character backstories were also a huge highlight.

Overall, Season 2 feels like a step forward in terms of story and structure. It’s very close, but because of the amount of strong moments, I’d say Season 2 is slightly better than Season 1.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

Season 2 really stepped up when it comes to major storylines.

The whole arc with Reese getting captured by the FBI was already insane and one of the biggest highlights of the season. Right after that, the storyline with his former partner Kara Stanton and the virus hit just as hard, especially because of how emotional and dark it was.

Then you also have Root’s entire plan to free the Machine, which slowly builds up over multiple episodes and leads into the finale. That whole storyline was very strong and added a lot to the overall plot, even if the final episode itself wasn’t quite as good as Season 1’s finale imo.

You can also clearly see how the show is moving away from purely episodic storytelling. Season 1 felt more like “one case per episode”, while Season 2 starts to connect everything into a bigger narrative, especially with the Machine and the backstories of the characters.

Overall, Season 2 just has more high points and a stronger ongoing story, even if Season 1 had the slightly better ending.

—————————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄—————————
This is a really great first season, honestly one of the best first seasons I’ve seen. Especially considering it has 23 episodes, it’s impressive how few filler episodes there are.

I’ve always liked those older 2010s shows with 20+ episodes per season, and this is a perfect example of why they can work so well.

Without going into spoilers, I can definitely recommend this series to anyone who enjoys action combined with a deeper and more complex story. The show follows two partners who solve crimes with the help of a Machine created by a programmer. They receive numbers and have to either protect that person or stop them from committing a crime. While this is the basic structure of each episode, the show gradually builds a larger overarching storyline.

—————————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑𝐒:—————————
In my opinion, this is easily one of the best first seasons I’ve watched, mainly because of the two main characters, Harold Finch and John Reese.

Both characters are extremely well written, especially when it comes to their backstories. Reese’s story stood out the most to me and was also the most emotional. The way he lost the woman he loved because he wasn’t there, and then was later betrayed and almost killed by the CIA, really adds depth to his character.

Finch’s story is also very interesting. While we don’t know everything yet, we do know that he created the Machine together with his partner Nathan Ingram, who seemingly died. Finch was also injured in the past, which explains why he has trouble walking.

What I found most fascinating is the Machine itself. It doesn’t just feel like a normal AI, but more like a living system that understands human behavior, which makes the whole concept even more compelling.

I also really liked the dynamics in the show. Not just between Reese and Finch, but also Reese with Carter and Fusco. The fact that they become part of the story and have their own arcs makes everything feel more connected.

The mafia storyline involving Elias, especially with Carter’s son being in danger, was also very strong and emotional.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑-𝐅𝐑𝐄𝐄——————

This was honestly such a strong first season. From the very first episode, the show instantly sets a dark tone and keeps building on it. The atmosphere is heavy, the animation is insanely good, and the fights are easily some of the best we’ve seen in Star Wars animation.

What surprised me the most is that it’s not just about Maul. The show actually focuses a lot on other characters too, which gives the story more depth and makes everything feel bigger.
The pacing is also really good. It never really slows down and just keeps delivering strong episodes one after another.

Overall, the season feels very intense, emotional at times, and visually insane. Definitely one of the best recent Star Wars projects imo.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

Maul was just insane this whole season. Every scene with him has aura, and I really like how the show makes him feel dangerous while still showing more emotional and human sides of him.
The whole storyline with Devon was really interesting. The way Maul manipulates everything, even going as far as letting her master die so she would follow him, was just cold but also really smart.

Two Boots also had a really good development. Seeing him slowly realize what the Empire actually is and then starting to help the others was great.
The Inquisitors were also really well done. They actually felt dangerous, especially characters like Marrok and the Eleventh Inquisitor.

Episode 9 was easily peak and the best of the whole series so far. Watching it on Star Wars Day made it even better. The fights were insane and that ending with Vader… yeah, he’s just different. Even the way he breathes is cold.
And the finale was just amazing but also kinda sad. The fights were again on another level and Maul’s strategy was really smart. I also really liked that he still doesn’t know who’s behind Vader’s mask, that adds a lot of tension for the future.
Lewon’s death also hit harder than expected.

Season 2 was honestly pretty disappointing for me compared to Season 1. It definitely still had some good moments, interesting ideas and strong atmosphere at times, but overall it felt way weaker and much less focused.
One of my biggest problems was that a lot of scenes felt extremely slow and dragged out. Many times the characters were just standing around talking instead of actually doing something, even during situations that were supposed to feel urgent.

There were still some things I liked though. The Titan lore, the Hollow Earth stuff and especially parts involving Bill Randa were interesting. The show also still looked visually great at times.
But overall I expected way bigger stakes, more payoff and especially a much stronger finale.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

The finale especially disappointed me. It didn’t feel like a real season finale at all and mostly just felt like setup for Season 3. I expected huge fights, massive reveals or at least some kind of crazy payoff, but instead it mostly just felt like “everything turned out fine.”

The whole “time travel” aspect also made less and less sense the longer the season went on. Some scenes near the end honestly just created plot holes and confusion for me instead of giving answers.
I also really didn’t care much about some of the human storylines this season. Kentaro’s plan near the end especially felt really weird and pointless to me.

That being said, the season still had some strong moments. Bill Randa discovering the Titan paths was cool and there were also a few really good episodes throughout the season.

But overall Season 2 just never reached the level of Season 1 for me and felt way more inconsistent. I wouldn’t even say Season 1 was amazing, but it was definitely better than this.

In my opinion this might honestly be the best season so far. The overall story was extremely strong and felt bigger than ever before. The season had some insane highs and some of the best moments in the entire show.

What I also really liked is how much darker and more intense the series has become. The stakes feel massive now and every episode pushes the overall story forward.

But despite all that, the animation still holds the season back for me. Even though I rated 4x7 a 9.9/10 and think the story is genuinely amazing, I still can’t give the season a perfect score. There are just way too many moments where characters barely move and scenes feel like PNGs sliding across the screen.
And honestly, having a filler episode in an 8-episode season was a really bad decision imo, especially because that episode was also by far the weakest and most boring one of the Show.

Still, the story, characters and overall scale of the season were so strong that I’d still call this an amazing season overall.

——————𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑——————

This season had some absolutely insane moments. The entire Viltrumite storyline was crazy and the introduction of Thragg completely changed the scale of the show. He instantly felt like the biggest threat in the entire series.
The “noodle scene” was honestly one of the most disturbing and brutal scenes the show has done so far. That whole episode was just insane.

I also really liked the ending and the deal with Mark, but that cliffhanger was crazy😭 now we have to wait another year again. Honestly, I’d even wait two years if it meant they could improve the animation quality.

Because as amazing as the story and fights were, there were still way too many awkward animation moments. Some scenes literally looked like moving PNGs and there were even moments where characters randomly disappeared or had the wrong face model. Stuff like that sadly happens way too often throughout the season.

The story itself though was genuinely fantastic. Nolan, Allen and especially Thragg carried so many scenes and Conquest was still an absolute monster whenever he appeared.
It’s now a 2:1 for Glenn.
Despite the animation issues, the writing and overall story progression were amazing and probably the strongest the show has ever been so far.

At the same time, the season isn’t perfect. Kevin is back in that “other place” and is immediately thrown into the water. He ends up in an old cabin, where he’s greeted by his former hunting buddy. His mission: kill the President. In return, Kevin wants to speak to the woman’s children, John’s child, and Christopher Sunday.

Shortly after, Kevin meets the man from the bridge again — the one who can make him sing. Then Kevin has to look into a glass panel and suddenly realizes: he himself is the President. And it gets even crazier. Whenever he looks through glass, he switches between two roles — the President and the assassin. Two versions of himself.

On top of that, Patti is the Secretary of Defense. She tells Kevin that he has to launch all the nuclear missiles and destroy the world. To do that, he has to cut a chip out of the heart of his identical twin — the assassin. Both Kevins sit across from each other, and neither of them actually wants this to happen.

The turning point comes with the suitcase Patti brings. Inside is Kevin’s diary. It describes his life, his time as a police officer, his inner emptiness, and his constant search for something he could never quite define. And most importantly: how he lost Nora.
That’s the moment both Kevins realize there’s no other way. Kevin cuts the chip out of his own heart.

An extremely emotional and brutal scene. Right after that, we see the missiles launching while Kevin and Patti stand on the roof, holding hands and watching it happen. Completely insane.

When Kevin wakes up again, he goes to his father, who is sitting on top of a house — because of the flood that never actually existed. It was all an illusion.

Suddenly, so much makes sense. For a long time, I thought this place was the afterlife or the place where the 2% disappeared. But it’s Kevin’s mind. He had to kill Patti — who never truly existed — to get her out of his head. He was shot, came back, and now he killed again because he believed he had nothing left to lose. He never truly believed in the flood — he lost Nora and thought this was how he could get her back.

Still, one big question remains:
Who is Kevin really?
Is he just a broken man? Or something divine? Was he chosen by God? Is he some kind of new Jesus — or just someone desperately trying to survive?

An unbelievably strong and brilliant episode.

The gang shooting also gave me a bit of that old Snowfall feeling again, which I really liked. So maybe this won’t just be about music, but also about how music connects to the gangs and the conflicts around them. That could actually be really interesting.

As a normal show about music and LA in the 90s, I think this could be really great. As a Snowfall spin-off though, I’m still not fully convinced yet.
